city.name: Chișinău
city.subtitle: Community, pogrom, ghetto and remembrance
city.description: Trace living synagogues and memorial landscapes of a city once central to Bessarabian Jewish life.

tour.title: Jewish Chișinău: Community, Pogrom and Remembrance
tour.subtitle: Five verified sites linking worship, violence and continuity
tour.overview: A city route connecting two active synagogues, the Jewish ghetto memorial, the historic cemetery and the memorial to victims of the 1903 pogrom.

stops.title: Chabad Lubavitch Central Synagogue — Glaziers' Synagogue
stops.shortDescription: The late nineteenth-century craftsmen's synagogue that remained legally open through the Soviet period.
stops.fullDescription: Built in 1888–98 for the glaziers' and bookbinders' society, this synagogue was the only Chișinău synagogue permitted to remain open after the Soviet closures of 1964. Now operated by Chabad, it preserves an active prayer hall and historic fabric. Entry requires advance security coordination.
stops.transcript: The Glaziers' Synagogue was built in the late nineteenth century by a society of Jewish glaziers and bookbinders. Occupational congregations were common in a city with dozens of Jewish prayer houses, schools and charitable associations. Its greatest historical distinction came under Soviet rule. In 1964 the authorities closed or repurposed Chișinău's other synagogues, while this building remained the city's only legally operating synagogue for more than four decades. Continuing prayer here therefore carried both religious and communal importance. Today Chabad-Lubavitch maintains the synagogue, mikveh and community activity. Look at the tall windows marking the prayer hall and women's gallery and remember that survival did not mean freedom from surveillance or restriction. This is a living, secure institution rather than an unrestricted monument. Arrange a visit before arriving and respect services. Beginning here prevents the tour from presenting Jewish Chișinău only through persecution: worship and community renewal continue in the city today.

stops.title: Sennaya Central Synagogue
stops.shortDescription: A restored nineteenth-century synagogue serving the Jewish Community of Moldova and Agudath Israel.
stops.fullDescription: The Sennaya synagogue was founded in 1886 and has been restored as an active synagogue and community centre. Its revival demonstrates the re-establishment of organised Jewish life after Soviet repression and large-scale emigration. Visitors must confirm access with the community.
stops.transcript: The Sennaya Synagogue dates its foundation to 1886, when Chișinău was a major centre of Bessarabian Jewish life. The city supported many prayer houses representing occupations, neighbourhoods and religious traditions. Soviet policy later closed and repurposed almost all of them, interrupting institutional continuity and leaving numerous buildings altered or lost. Restoration of Sennaya as an active synagogue and community centre therefore represents more than architectural repair. It provides space for prayer, study, volunteering and a renewed sense of belonging among Jews in Moldova. The Jewish Community of the Republic of Moldova connects congregations and organisations across the country, while this site provides a visible centre in the capital. Do not treat recovery as a simple return to the past: the population, languages and social conditions have changed profoundly. Arrange entry in advance and comply with security. Together with the Glaziers' Synagogue, Sennaya shows that heritage includes contemporary choices to rebuild Jewish institutions, not only the conservation of ruins.

stops.title: Monument to the Victims of the Chișinău Ghetto
stops.shortDescription: A memorial at the former ghetto entrance remembering Jews confined, murdered and deported under Romanian and German occupation.
stops.fullDescription: Established in 1992, the memorial by sculptor Naum Epelbaum and architect Semion Șoihet stands near an entrance to the ghetto created in July 1941. Thousands were imprisoned before mass shootings and deportations to Transnistria. An information panel maps the ghetto boundary.
stops.transcript: This memorial stands near an entrance to the ghetto imposed after Romanian and German forces occupied Chișinău in July 1941. More than eleven thousand Jews were crowded into a poor section of the city behind fencing and barbed wire. Hunger, disease and shootings killed many, while deportations across the Dniester into Romanian-administered Transnistria exposed prisoners to further violence, starvation and death. The monument, created by Naum Epelbaum and Semion Șoihet, shows a grieving figure before a pierced Star of David. Inscriptions address the martyrs and victims and declare that the living remember them. A nearby panel helps restore the vanished ghetto to the modern street plan. Avoid using imprecise phrases that hide responsibility: Romanian authorities administered the ghetto in alliance with Nazi Germany. Stand quietly and consider that ordinary streets around you became instruments of confinement. The memorial opened after the Soviet period, when fuller public discussion of specifically Jewish suffering became possible.

stops.title: Chișinău Jewish Cemetery
stops.shortDescription: A vast nineteenth-century cemetery with tens of thousands of burials, a ruined funeral hall and monuments to communal leaders and pogrom victims.
stops.fullDescription: The cemetery contains an estimated 40,000–50,000 burials and has lost parts of its original territory to development. It includes the grave of Chief Rabbi Yehuda Leib Tsirelson, a ruined ceremonial building and extensive inscriptions documenting Bessarabian Jewish life. Conservation remains an active challenge.
stops.transcript: The Chișinău Jewish Cemetery is one of the city's largest surviving archives of Jewish life. Burials began here in the nineteenth century, and estimates place forty to fifty thousand graves within the remaining grounds. Hebrew, Yiddish, Russian and Romanian inscriptions record rabbis, craftspeople, soldiers, parents and children. Among the best-known graves is that of Rabbi Yehuda Leib Tsirelson, chief rabbi of Bessarabia and an important religious leader. A ruined ceremonial structure and damaged monuments also reveal decades of neglect, vandalism and territorial loss. Part of the old cemetery was cleared during the Soviet period, and urban development continues to press against the site. Government and heritage initiatives have proposed conservation, but the scale is immense. Visit as a cemetery, not an abandoned attraction: dress respectfully, avoid stepping on graves, do not remove anything and give mourners privacy. The names here restore individuality to a community too often described only through population totals and catastrophe.

stops.title: 1903 Pogrom Victims Memorial — Alunelul Park
stops.address: Alunelul Park, Calea Ieșilor, Chișinău, Moldova
stops.shortDescription: A memorial on former cemetery land remembering those murdered in the 1903 and 1905 anti-Jewish pogroms.
stops.fullDescription: The memorial was initiated in 1993 and expanded for the centenary of the 1903 Kishinev pogrom. The violence killed 49 Jews in 1903 and another 19 in 1905, injured hundreds and became an international symbol of antisemitic persecution in the Russian Empire. The park itself occupies part of the former cemetery.
stops.transcript: Alunelul Park occupies land once belonging to the Jewish cemetery, so the setting itself forms part of the memorial history. In April 1903, rumours and organised antisemitic incitement preceded two days of attacks on Jewish residents. Forty-nine Jews were killed, hundreds were injured, homes and businesses were destroyed, and authorities failed to stop the violence. A second pogrom in 1905 killed another nineteen Jews. News of Kishinev spread internationally through journalism, protest meetings, poetry and relief campaigns. The events influenced Jewish political thought, self-defence organisations and migration, while becoming a warning about what official tolerance of hatred could produce. The memorial uses restrained stone rather than dramatic reconstruction. Read it alongside the surrounding park and remember that part of the cemetery was erased during Soviet redevelopment. This final stop connects violence, burial and urban memory: the city changed the landscape, but descendants and community organisations returned names and meaning to it.
